exercise1.prompt: comments about virtual environments, then an explanation

cases.name: a comment explains what a virtual environment is

hiddenCases.name: the printed text is about dependencies
hiddenCases.describe: an explanation mentioning dependencies or packages

exercise1.hint: The comment says what a virtual environment is; the print says why it helps when two projects want different versions of the same package.

exercise2.prompt: comments about requirements.txt, then an explanation

hiddenCases.name: the printed text is about reproducing the setup
hiddenCases.describe: an explanation of what the file buys you

exercise2.hint: requirements.txt is the list; pip install -r is what reads it. The print should say why writing the list down matters.

questions.prompt: What problem does a virtual environment solve?
choices: Python programs run faster inside one
Two projects can need different versions of the same package
It hides your source code from other users
It removes the need for pip
questions.explain: One machine, one shared set of installed packages, two projects that disagree about a version. A virtual environment gives each project its own set.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you would actually do them.
questions.explain: Create it, step into it, then install. Freezing before installing anything records an empty list, which helps nobody.

questions.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
right: Writes down what is installed right now
questions.explain: The last two are a pair: one records the environment, the other rebuilds it somewhere else.

questions.prompt: Why does a project commit requirements.txt but not the .venv folder?
choices: The file is a short, readable list of what is needed
The folder holds installed binaries that differ between machines
Anyone can rebuild the folder from the file
questions.explain: The recipe is worth sharing; the meal is not. Anyone with the recipe can cook it on their own machine.
